symptom_summary: History is a `view` state inside the single overlay BrowserWindow (not a separate window/tray item/hotkey). Every History entry point (Bar/RightEdgeSidecar History button, Escape-from-Review, Review's own exits) routes through a dirty-Review guard that calls the browser-native, blocking `window.confirm()` on a frame:false, transparent, setAlwaysOnTop(true,'screen-saver') window inside an LSUIElement/accessory app with no Dock icon. The team's own code comment (index.ts:8434-8439) documents that a dialog with no properly attached parent window on this exact app type "hangs forever with no error and no visible dialog" -- and that lesson was applied to every main-process dialog.showMessageBox call except the renderer's window.confirm sites. The result: an unanswerable, invisible confirm dialog blocks the renderer thread forever, there is no recovery path for 'unresponsive' (unlike the existing render-process-gone auto-reload), and ensureWindow()/second-instance never check isResponsive(), so a relaunch attempt during the freeze is a silent no-op -- reproducing "it's running but it just doesn't open the app again" exactly. A secondary, latent (not yet triggered at Tony's current 59-file/892KB library) architectural issue: History-list/search re-reads and re-decrypts the entire meeting library on every call with unbounded concurrency, on the main process.

root_causes.title: No recovery path exists for an 'unresponsive' (wedged-but-alive) renderer -- only actual crashes self-heal
root_causes.mechanism: win.on('render-process-gone', ...) has a full recovery path (resets state, self.loadURL to reload). win.on('unresponsive', ...) only logs a warning and writes an audit event -- no timeout, no forced reload, no destroy-and-recreate. If the renderer never becomes responsive again (e.g. because of RC1's unanswerable dialog), the window is wedged for the life of the process with nothing to unstick it.

code_evidence.note: win.on('unresponsive', ...) only mainLog.warn + auditLog -- no recovery action
win.webContents.on('render-process-gone', ...) DOES self-heal via self.loadURL(overlayRendererUrl()) at line 2782 -- the asymmetry

root_causes.repro_steps: Trigger RC1 (or any other renderer-blocking synchronous call). Wait past the 'unresponsive' event firing. Confirm no further audit.log events (app.crash, reload, etc.) are ever written for that window -- only Force Quit ends it.

root_causes.regression_test: Contract test asserting that a webContents 'unresponsive' event with no 'responsive' event within the grace window triggers the same reload/recreate call render-process-gone's handler makes, and that an audit event is recorded.

root_causes.title: ensureWindow()/second-instance never check webContents.isResponsive(), so a relaunch cannot detect or heal a wedged window

root_causes.title: listMeetings()/searchMeetings() do an uncapped-concurrency full-library rescan on every History open/search keystroke, on the main process
root_causes.mechanism: Both functions do `await Promise.all((await meetingFiles(folder)).map((f) => readMeeting(folder, f)))` -- reading, AES-GCM-decrypting, and regex-parsing (searchMeetings additionally full-text-scanning) every saved meeting file concurrently with no batching/cap, on the main process via ipcMain.handle. A per-file (mtimeMs,size) cache makes repeat calls on an unchanged library cheap, but the first call each session (or after any file change) still fires this unbounded scan. Not today's acute trigger (Tony's real meetings folder has only 59 files / 892KB, counted without reading content), but it is a latent scalability/reliability defect: as the library grows, History-open latency degrades linearly with zero backpressure, and because it runs on the single-threaded main process that also owns tray/hotkey/second-instance dispatch, a slow scan would stall the WHOLE app, not just the History panel.

root_causes.mechanism: resumeBackfillIfPending() (called unconditionally 15s after every boot) invokes startBackfill() with no options, i.e. respectRetryBackoff=false/undefined. root_causes.title: unhandledRejection is logged as app.crash even though the process never dies (false crash detection)
root_causes.mechanism: onFatal() is registered as the process's unhandledRejection listener. The process keeps running. root_causes.title: render-process-gone reloads the window unconditionally with no crash-loop breaker or user-facing recovery surface
root_causes.mechanism: The render-process-gone handler always calls self.loadURL(overlayRendererUrl()) again, with no check on details.reason, no counter of prior occurrences, no backoff, and no ceiling after which it stops and shows the user something. If the same condition that killed the renderer recurs immediately after reload (resource pressure, a poison piece of persisted state), this becomes an invisible, unbounded reload loop. root_causes.title: The boot-incomplete sentinel is cleared (near-instantly, at registerIpc) before the 15-second-delayed brain-resume step it was documented to protect, so the crash class it was built for (MQA-175) can silently escape detection at HEAD
root_causes.mechanism: clearBootWatchOnce() is guarded by a single module-local bootWatchClosed flag - first caller wins, every later caller is a no-op. On a normal boot the registerIpc caller fires within milliseconds of beginBootWatch, so the sentinel file is deleted almost immediately. But the actual dangerous work the sentinel's own doc comment names as its reason for existing - the .brain/index.json OSCrypt decrypt inside the brain resume/backfill/reconcile step - only runs 15 seconds later, and its own clearBootWatchOnce('mqa-175') call is a no-op because the flag is already set. So if that exact native crash happens today during the 15s-delayed brain resume, boot-incomplete.json is already gone, and the next launch will report no earlyDeath at all for it - the opposite failure mode from a false positive: a false negative on the one crash class this file exists to catch. Separately, and more narrowly, everything between beginBootWatch and registerIpc is synchronous with no blocking awaits in the normal path, so a force-quit landing in that specific window (the task's original hypothesis) requires either exquisite timing or one of the runStep-wrapped synchronous calls (createTray/registerShortcuts, unbudgeted) running slowly.

code_evidence.note: const clearBootWatchOnce = (reason) => { if (bootWatchClosed) return; bootWatchClosed = true; ... endBootWatch(...) } - single shared latch across five different callers

clearBootWatchOnce('mqa-175') inside the 15-second setTimeout's finally block - a no-op on essentially every real boot because 9288 already closed the watch

root_causes.title: No SIGTERM handler and non-detached sidecar spawn mean a hard-killed session leaves orphaned llama-server/Crashpad-handler processes with no boot-time reaper to clean them up
root_causes.mechanism: local-runtime.ts spawns llama-server via plain child_process.spawn with no detached flag, so its lifetime is only tied to the parent by JS code that explicitly kills it. That JS code lives exclusively in graceful-quit paths (before-quit, will-quit, the app's own emergency-quit hotkey) which are Electron application-level lifecycle events, not OS signal handlers. The app registers no process.on('SIGTERM', ...) anywhere, so an external SIGTERM (kill without -9, many process-manager/logout paths) terminates the process immediately via Node's default action, skipping every cleanup path; a SIGKILL (Activity Monitor Force Quit) is uncatchable by any process by definition. Either way the child is not killed, and since it was never detached it simply reparents to launchd (ppid=1) instead of dying with its parent - exactly E2's observation of two orphaned llama-server processes plus orphaned chrome_crashpad_handler processes. There is no boot-time scan that finds and kills a previous session's stale sidecars before spawning a new one.

code_evidence.note: proc = spawn(binaryPath, args, { stdio: ['ignore','pipe','pipe'], windowsHide: true, env: {...} }) - no detached key, default false

function stopSidecarsForHardExit(): kills screenPreprocess/localRuntime/fmRuntime and calls endBootWatch - but this is JS invoked only from the app's own emergency-quit hotkey path, never from an OS signal
app.on('will-quit', ...) - the other place sidecar teardown + endBootWatch happen; also gated on the JS event loop running, i.e. Electron's own quit lifecycle, not an OS signal

root_causes.fix: Add process.on('SIGTERM', () => app.quit()) (and SIGINT for dev) next to the existing uncaughtException/unhandledRejection registrations, converting any catchable external termination into the existing, already-tested clean-quit path. Separately, add a boot-time reaper that identifies and kills this app's own stale llama-server/chrome_crashpad_handler processes left over from a previous hard-kill (e.g. via a pid file local-runtime.ts writes next to boot-incomplete.json) before spawning a fresh sidecar.
root_causes.regression_test: Source-contract test asserting a SIGTERM handler exists and calls app.quit. Integration-style test for the reaper: stand up a fake pidfile plus a spawned no-op sleeper process representing a stale llama-server, assert the reaper kills only the process it can positively prove is stale (matching this app's own recorded pid) and never touches an unrelated process.

   - Adding `process.on('SIGTERM', () => app.quit())` would only replace Electron's handler with an equivalent one. The proposed source-contract test would lock in dead code.

When main dies for any reason, including SIGKILL, the pipe closes, `cat` gets EOF, and the server is killed. Keep port parsing on the child's stdout and stderr, and keep `LLAMA_API_KEY` in env.

verifications.evidence:
The symptom is real: sidecars are orphaned and nothing cleans them up at the next launch. But the mechanism is wrong on SIGTERM, on the detached flag, and on Crashpad. Both parts of the SIGTERM fix are redundant or harmful.

WHAT HOLDS UP
- src/main/llm/local-runtime.ts:362 calls spawn() without detached. There is no boot-time reaper. A grep for reap/pidfile/pkill/orphan under src/main found only temp-file and draft sweeps (index.ts:8965-8966).
- The only process-level handlers are uncaughtException and unhandledRejection (index.ts:8949-8950). Sidecar teardown happens only in will-quit (index.ts:9461-9517) and in stopSidecarsForHardExit (index.ts:4169). Both are JS code.
- ps on the live machine (run outside the sandbox, read-only): llama-server 5489 (ppid 1, pgid 1468, started 13:54:33 EDT) and llama-server 8347 (ppid 1, pgid 8075, started 14:03:53 EDT). The current main process is 9125, started 14:10:19 EDT, and its own llama-server 47256 is a normal child.
- Each orphan's pgid equals the pid of the dead main process. The orphans belong to the sessions that started at 17:47Z and 18:03Z.
- The leak is large. `footprint` reports phys_footprint 3124 MB for each orphan (top: 3120M compressed, 0% CPU). That is about 6.2 GB for the two, which directly feeds the "heavy on the PC" report.
- The port is ephemeral (--port 0) and each session has its own key, so an orphan only wastes resources. It never conflicts with the new session.

WHAT IS WRONG
1) The claim that SIGTERM hits Node's default action and skips cleanup is false. I ran a probe on the repo's Electron 43.6.0 with no process.on('SIGTERM'). A single SIGTERM logged "before-quit | will-quit"; afterwards both the main process and its child were gone. Electron installs its own signal handler that routes SIGTERM into the normal quit sequence.
   While the main thread was hung, the first SIGTERM was queued and did nothing. The second one killed the process at once, and the child was orphaned.
   So process.on('SIGTERM', () => app.quit()) is redundant when the app is responsive. When the app is hung it cannot run at all, because JS is blocked. Registering it through libuv would also likely override Electron's handler and stop a repeated SIGTERM from killing a hung app.
2) The detached flag makes no difference. On macOS a child never dies with its parent; detached:true only calls setsid. My SIGKILL probe reproduced the exact pattern seen live: the child got ppid 1 and a pgid equal to the dead main pid.
3) The Crashpad handlers are not independent orphans. ppid 1 is by design; the current session's handler 9128 also has ppid 1, as do the handlers for Chrome, Claude and Plaud. In the probe with crashReporter.start({uploadToServer:false}), matching index.ts:944, the handler stayed alive exactly as long as the orphaned child did and exited once that child was killed. The likely reason is that the child inherits the parent's crash-reporting connection.
   The stale handlers 1477 and 8081 map one-to-one onto the sessions of orphans 5489 and 8347. Reaping chrome_crashpad_handler by name would therefore be wrong and would hit other apps.
4) The inferences drawn from E3 and E8 are wrong.
   - E3: the code emits no clean-shutdown audit event at all. The app.* events that exist are started, boot.watch_cleared, crash, recovery, renderer.ready and unresponsive. Also, kern.boottime and `last reboot` show a system reboot at 2026-09-25 13:46:15 EDT (17:46Z) with no shutdown record, so the gap between 17:42Z and 17:47Z is an unclean OS restart, not a force-quit.
   - E8: the idle stop logs 'idle' (local-runtime.ts:300) and then stop() logs 'explicit' (:638). The audit log shows that pair 8 ms apart at 18:27:35Z, so stops are over-counted.

WHAT THE AUDIT LOG SAYS ABOUT HOW THE TWO SESSIONS DIED
- stop() writes 'local.runtime.stop explicit' through a synchronous file transport (logger.ts:309-312) whenever the runtime was running.
- There is no such event between local.runtime.start at 17:54:52Z and the next app.started at 18:03:25Z. There is none between 18:04:09Z and 18:10:20Z either. So neither will-quit nor stopSidecarsForHardExit ran.
- There is no app.crash on 09-25 after 12:13:56Z, so this was not the onFatal path. E7 lists no Crashpad dump for 09-25, so it was not a native crash.
- The pattern fits SIGKILL (Force Quit), or two SIGTERMs sent to a hung main process. No JS inside the dying process can run in either case.

CODE PATH THE HYPOTHESIS MISSED
index.ts:3575-3576: when the uncaughtException dialog's "Relaunch Métis" is chosen, the code calls app.relaunch() then app.exit(0) without calling stopSidecarsForHardExit(). app.exit skips will-quit (index.ts:4164 says so), so this path orphans llama-server, fm-serve and the screen watcher.
verifications.corrected_mechanism_or_fix:
Corrected mechanism: the app hangs and the user force-quits it. That is SIGKILL, or a second SIGTERM sent while the main thread is blocked; Electron already handles the first SIGTERM through the normal before-quit/will-quit sequence. Either way the process dies without running any JS teardown. On macOS the llama-server child survives with ppid 1, whatever the detached flag says. It keeps its roughly 3.1 GB footprint and also keeps that session's Crashpad handler alive, until reboot, because nothing at launch finds and kills it. Fix:
1) Do NOT add process.on('SIGTERM'). It is redundant, and likely harmful because it would override Electron's native handler.
2) Add a launch-time reaper that runs before the first sidecar spawn:
   - local-runtime.ts writes {pid, start time, binary path} to userData/sidecars/llama.pid after spawning and deletes it in stop().
   - At boot, if the recorded pid is alive, check three things before sending SIGKILL: its executable path equals this app's resolved llama-server binary, its start time matches the recorded one (to guard against pid reuse), and its ppid is 1.
   - Do the same for fm-serve and the screen-preprocess watcher.
   - Never reap by name, and never touch chrome_crashpad_handler: it exits by itself once the orphan dies.

4) Optional: stop logging the stop twice on idle.

Tests:
- Source-contract test that every app.exit( call site is preceded by stopSidecarsForHardExit().
- Reaper test using a pidfile plus a spawned sleeper. Check three cases: the sleeper is killed when path and start time match; it is left alone when the start time does not match (pid reuse); and a pid belonging to an unrelated process is never touched.

The boot-sentinel (boot-early-death/safe_start) mechanism is soundly designed for its one documented native-crash class but its multi-site clearBootWatchOnce race now closes the watched window before the 15-second-delayed brain-resume step it was built to protect, so it may be silently under-protecting the exact crash it exists for. One historical minidump (July 2026, v1.3.0) shows a genuine native crash class (Metis Helper utility process refused Library Validation) that HEAD's entitlements appear to already fix, pending packaging-lane verification. No macOS .ips crash reports exist at all - essentially everything in audit.log's app.crash tally is a JS-level event, not a native OS-level crash.
